Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
whether it is a fact that capital of Foreign financial Institutions (FFIs) during the year 2007-

if so, the amount of capital brought in India by these FFIs between April to June, July to 
September and October to December, 2007; 
whether it is also a fact that foreign capital has been collected by respective institutions during 
each of the said period; and

THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (d) A Statement is 
laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) There is no entity formally defined as a Foreign Financial Institution (FFI). FFIs
are understood as foreign banks and foreign Non-Banking Finance Companies (NBFCs). 
The minimum capital requirements stipulated by Reserve Bank of India (RBI) require a 
foreign bank opening a branch in India to bring in US $25 million as an assigned capital. 
Foreign banks are also required to maintain minimum capital funds amounting to not less 
than 9 per cent of Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) of its Indian operations. 
Further, the minimum capitalization norms stipulated for setting up a 100% operating 
subsidiary (NBFC) by foreign investors in US$ 50 million. The capital foreign banks and

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: I would require a separate question if the question 
relates to Foreign Institutional Investors. The question that came to us, both in the draft 
form and in the printed version, is about Foreign Financial Institutions, and I have given the 
answer. But if the question has to be asked about FIIs, I have told my dear friend, please put 
a separate question. 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: But the Minister is well-versed with the 
statistics. 
SHRI R CHIDAMBARAM: I can give the policy, but how can I give the figures. I don't 
carry the figures with me. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Would like to ask the second supplementary. 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: No. The printers' devil has saved the Minister. 
SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: Whatever the comedy of errors, at least, the answer is very 
specific and very useful and thank you, very much for the information that you have supplied. 
I just want to ask: Has the Reserve Bank of India or any part of your Ministry developed any 
mechanism to assess the effect of this massive infusion of foreign funds on our economic 
development and particularly determining the end use of this money? 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, firstly, it is wrong to say that there is a massive infusion 
of foreign funds. As far as the banking sector is concerned, the policy is that we will have 
public sector banks, Indian private sector banks and foreign banks. All three kinds of 
banks will compete with each other and that will not only expand the banking system, but it 
will also improve the efficiency, bring new products to the market, spread the banking 
habits and make available banking products to the people of India. The capital that has been 
brought by Foriegn Financial Institutions, which is foreign banks plus NBFCs, is, as on 
December 31,2007, only about Rs. 26,000 crores, which is about 4 billion dollars. The size 
of our banking industry is much larger than that. The size of our economy is a trillion dollars, 

Oral Answers [22 APRIL 2008] to Questions   7 
that is, 1000 billion dollars. I don't think that there is a massive infusion of foreign funds. 
Just as Indian banks are establishing branches abroad and expanding overseas, foreign banks 
would also have to be allowed to establish branches in India and expand in India. In an 
integrated world, it is not possible to say that Indian banks should open branches in other 
countries, but the banks of other countries will not be allowed to open branches here. 
SHRI M.V. MYSURA REDDY: I want to know from the Finance Minister whether the 
foreign banks have complained about priority sector norms applicable to India banks. Are 
there any special regulatory privileges or exemptions enjoyed by the foreign banks versus 
Indian banks? If yes, why should such regulatory privileges or exemptions be granted to 
foreign banks? 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: The guidelines for foreign banks are slightly different from 
the guidelines for the Indian banks. The principal reason is that we do not allow foreign 
banks to establish branches in rural areas. It is very rarely that branch licences are granted to 
foreign banks to establish branches in rural areas. In fact, we find that most of the branches 
of the foreign banks are in Tier-I towns. In the last three years, for example, most of the 
foreign bank branches have been given in Mumbai, Kolkata, Noida, Ahmedabad, Chennai, 
etc. therefore, the same norms cannot be applied to foriegn banks. In fact, if you allow them 
to open branches in rural areas, then, surely, we can ask them to follow the same norms, but 
for reasons which are otherwise well known, we are very restrictive about allowing foreign 
banks to go into rural areas.

Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
whether Government has been able to check the inflation rate which has touched a 59-
week high of 6.7 per cent as on 15 March, 2008 and inflation is likely to remain at 
elevated levels between 6.7 per cent and 7.4 per cent; 
if so, the details thereof during the last three years on quarterly basis till date; 
whether Reserve Bank of India has apprehended any upward pressure of inflation; and 
if so, the details thereof and the steps taken by Government, till date in this regard keeping 
in view that wholesale price-based inflation rate has already jumped 1.5 percentage points 
through first fortnight of March, 2008?

Statement

as on 15 March, 2008 and reached to 7.4 per cent on March 29,2008, However, it has come 
down to 7.1 per cent as on April 5, 2008. Quarterly inflation in terms of Wholesale Price 
Index (WPI) of the last three years is indicated in the table 1.

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, I am grateful to the hon. Member for putting a very 
exhaustive question. Only last week, we had a full discussion in this House on price rise, 
and, perhaps the hon. Member was not present at that time, or, did not have the opportunity 
to participate in the debate. We have explained the Government's position on this matter. 
There was a full-scale debate. I intervened in the debate and the Minister for Agriculture 
replied to the debate. Between then and now, I have nothing new to add except to say that as 
and when necessary, more fiscal measures will be taken. We have taken a set of fiscal measures 
and some more fiscal measures are being contemplated. 
As far as monetary measures are concerned, the day after the debate concluded, the Reserve 
Bank increased the CRR by 50 basis points in two instalments, and, that has been widely 
published in the newspapers. The monetary policy review is coming up on the 29th of April, 
and, one would have to wait to see what further steps the Reserve Bank takes. 
As far as administrative measures are concerned, we have already banned the export of 
wheat, non-basmati rice and pulses. In order to augment domestic availability, and, if there 
are no other downsides to banning some other commodities, we will certainly consider any 
suggestions in that behalf. But as, I submitted during the debate, it will take sometime for 
fiscal and monetary measures to take effect. 
As far as cartels are concerned, it is my view that the cement manufacturers, and, to some 
extent, the steel manufacturers are behaving like cartels. Some enquiries have been 
commenced by the MRTP. We are looking at the legal and the adminsitrative provisions that 
are available to the Government. The Ministry of Industry and the Ministry of Steel are also 
talking to the steel producers and the cement producers. When steps are taken, certainly, we 
will take the House into confidence and report the steps to the House. In the meanwhile, if 
there are any specific suggestions from the hon. Member, whom I hold in great regard, I 
would be very happy to consider those suggestions and respond to them.

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, action against hoarders and black marketeers can be 
taken under the Essential Commodities Act. It is my understanding of the Essential 
Commodities Act that these powers are available to the State Government. Earlier, the position 
was that control orders could not be passed by the State Government without prior approval 
of the Central Government. That position was amended by the UPA Government and we 
have restored the powers to the State Government to pass control orders without obtaining 
prior approval of the Central Government. Therefore, whatever action needs to be taken 
against hoarders-big or small, names don't matter-these actions have to be taken by the State 
Governments. I have with me a list of actions taken by different State Governments during 
calendar 2007. During the debate, I did refer to this list and I am willing to refer to this list. 
Most of the action has been taken only in a few States. There have been only a small number 
of prosecutions and an even smaller number of convictions. I am already on record in this 
House and I would once again on record to state this. I would urge the State Governments to 
use all the powers available to them under the Essential Commodities Act, take action against 
hoarders, black marketeers and profiteers, prosecute them and convict them.

MR. CHAIRMAN: Now, Question No. 404. 
Funds for the weaker sections 
*404.     SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE:tt
SHRI GIRESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
whether Government has announced that it would set up two funds with a total corpus of Rs. 
1,000 crore for greater financial inclusion of weaker sections of the society through 
development work, each with a corpus of Rs. 500 crore, of which a maximum of Rs. 200 
crore each whould be contributed by the Centre over a period of five years: 
whether during 2007-08, he had announced constitution of Financial Inclusion Fund and 
Financial Inclusion Technology Fund with an overall corpus of Rs. 500 crore each with 
initial funding from Government, RBI and the NABARD; and 
the extent to which the funds had been utilised so far? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN 
KUMAR BANSAL): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shrimati Supriya Sule.

14    Oral, Answers [RAJYA SABHA] to Questions 
Statement 
(a) and (b) In the Union Budget 2007-08, it was announced that a Financial Inclusion
Fund for meeting the cost of developmental and promotional interventions and a Financial 
Inclusion Technology Fund to meet the cost of technology adoption, each with an overall 
corpus of Rs. 500 crore, with initial funding to be contributed by the Central Government, 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development 
(NABARD), will be established. 
Both the Funds have been constituted in NABARD. Government of India and NABARD 
have made an initial contribution of Rs. 10 crore and Rs. 5 crore respectively, in each Fund 
in March, 2008. RBI is expected to contribute its matching share of Rs. 10 crore in each 
Fund shortly. 
(c) Both the Funds have been established recently and utilisation of Funds will commence
in 2008-09. 
SHR1MATI SUPRIYA SULE: Sir, part (c) of the reply says that utilisation of Funds 
will commence in 2008-09. Could the hon. Minister kindly tell us the criteria and priority 
laid down in this Fund? Could he give some more details regarding disbursement of this 
Fund? 
SHRI PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL: Sir, the final report which has been received makes 
various recommendations under which the funds can be utilised. First is that the Regional 
Rural Banks etc. will also fix up their targets for utilisations. Sir. the separate category of 
micro finance etc has been set up. National Calamity Relief Fund will also address this 
problem. And the guidelines which further talk of the objectives and the eligible activities. 
Sir, I would just let those know. The first to that effect is that capacity building inputs to 
business facilitators and business correspondents which the banks are engaging to expand 
the network of the banks, to take the banks to their doorsteps; then, Sir, to provide promotional 
support to institutions such as Resource Centres Farmers Service Centres, Farmers Clubs 
Self Employment Training Institutions etc., as also the Self Help Groups and the capacity 
building of personnel in the NABARD, in the banks, in the post offices, State Government 
departments, MFIs, i.e. Micro Finance Institutions, the NGOs, the local level associations. 
The Self Help Groups, Joint Liability Groups etc. who are to be roped in to expand the 
objective of the financial inclusion would all be part of it. And, then, this supporting initiative 
of the local level associations; then, support pilot projects for development of innovative 
products, processes and prototype of financial inclusion. Sir, this is as far as the Financial 
Inclusion Fund is concerned. 
When it comes to the Financial Inclusion Technology Fund,.... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: I think the question has been answered. 
SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: Sir, I am satisfied with the reply. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Second supplementary, please,.. (Interruptions)... 
SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: Thank you, Sir, for the detail reply. Since you have brought 
up SHGs, I Would like to ask this question. We have a longstanding demand for all the SHG 
to get good quality training from the Government and give us a lower interest rate. The 
interest rate which is anywhere between nine and twelve should be lowered to four. So, if 
you are making this for the weaker sections of the society, would you look into it and take 
into consideration all our demands, especially the ones made for Self Help Groups? 

Oral Answers  [22 APRIL 2008]  to Questions   15  
SHRI PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL: Sir as far as training of the Self Help Groups is 
concerned, that is an ongoing activity. Presently also, the banks are seriously engagaed in 
that, that the capacity of the Self Help Groups should be built up, that the absorptive capacity 
of the people who take the loan should be built up. And the story of these Self Help Groups 
is, indeed, a story of success. Today, we have as many as 30 lakh Self Help Groups, which 
means over four crore people are already engagaed in this process. Sir, as far as the question 
of interest is concerned, that is from case to case; when the banks really discuss, there are 
certain issues. When it comes to the banks, banks take their own decisions.  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Thank you.  
SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: But, Sir, if this Fund is meant for helping the Self Help 
Groups, why not make certain considerations especially for the weaker sections of the society?  
SHRI PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL: This Fund is different from the other things. In this 
Fund, Sir, there is a different provision. The Advisory Board has been set up; it will be for 
the Advisory Board to consider. The funds will vest with the NABARD. But this Advisory 
Board to consider of eleven important, senior people. Every application will be discussed by 
them, and according to that, the funds will be made available to them. ...(Interruptions)...  
SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: What about the commitment, Sir?  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Shri Gireesh Kumar Sanghi....  
SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: Sir, you have to give some commitment. ...(Interruptions)...  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Mr. Sanghi, please. (Interruptions)...  
SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI; Sir, a recent data released by the National Sample 
Survey Organisation says that nine out of ten unorg anised units are starved of finances. It 
also says that 92 per cent of unorganised enterpris es in India do not receive any financial 
assistance from banks or any other sources, reflecting a poor state of financial inclusion in 
our country; these enterprises are something like 20 millions in the country, and they employ 
more than 40 million people. My questions to the ho n. Minister are, what is the specific 
target of SHGs that he is setting up to include all  the smaller and medium enterprises and 
whether there is any specific programme by the Government to include the weaker sections 
of the society as "the most backward'? And what is the total percentage of population who 
are not included in the financial system or who have no access to the financial assistance?  
SHRI PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL: Sir, this question relates  to financial inclusion and 
the two Funds set up to promote financial inclusion. Sir, the date that we have presently for 
this question relates to the extent of financial in clusion as far as the rural households are 
concerned. Sir, the total number of rural household s that we have is 893.5 lakhs, and I 
would, with all the humility, like to correct one statement made by the hon. Member when he 
says that it is 92 per cent of the rural households  who are financially excluded. It is not 92. 
Sir. Actually, it is 51.4 per cent of the households who don't have any access to loans either ' 
from the financial institutions or from the private  sources. Twenty-seven per cent of those 
have access to the formal sources. About one-third of those also approach the informal 
sources. From that you can infer, Sir, that 72.7 pe r cent of the households do not have any 
form of access to the financial institutions. Initi ally it was fixed that only one district in 
every State had to be covered. But now the banks ha ve taken it up in the mission mode and 
a large number of banks are reporting that it is not just one district in a State, but a large  

16    Oral Answers [RAJYA SABHA] to Questions 
number of districts. At least, three States have declared 100 per cent financial inclusion 
meaning thereby that every household in the State has a low frills account where they don't 
have to have any balance or the minimum balance and that entitles them to certain other 
access to credit.

Involvement of airlines in human trafficking 
*405.     SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA:††
SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHART1A: 
Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to state: 
whether the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) is aware that staff of various 
airlines are involved in human trafficking; 
if so, the details thereof; 
whether Government proposes to put a check on the activities of staff of various airlines 
posted at airports/planes; and 
if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI 
PRAFUL PATEL): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) DGCA is not concerned with the matter of human trafficking. However, as per
information received from Mumbai Police one Air Hostess and one Flight Purser were arrested 
by Detective Crime Branch, Criminal Investigation Department in C.R. No. 120/07. The Air 
Hostess employed with Jet Airways, and the Flight Purser employed with Inter Global Air 
transport, New Delhi were involved in cheating and forgery case, by way of abetting to get 
U.S. Visa to the persons desiring to migrate from India to U.S.A.  
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Vijay Jf, Darda

Oral Answers [22 APRIL 2008] to Questions   19 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. Bureau, of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS) by way of formulating
procedures and measures on aviation security in compliance with the National Civil Aviation 
Security Programme approved by the Government, has taken adequate and effective steps to 
check on the activities of staff of various airlines posted at Airports/planes. Security 
Programme for airlines has to be approved by the BCAS before obtaining the Operator 
Permit. Background of employees of airlines/airport operator are being verified by local 
police/intelligence agencies before issuing Airport Entry Passes (AEPs) to them. Regular 
Aviation Security Audit, Inspections, Tests are being conducted by BCAS for each and every 
airlines/airport to ensure compliance of aviation security standards and procedures. 
Compliance of all orders/instructions issued by BCAS is mandatory for all airlines.

Threat of Global Warming 
*01. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be
pleased to state: 
whether India has geared up to meet acute water shortage in view of the threat of global 
warming; 
if so, the details thereof; and 
if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ): (a) to (c) 
Realising the need for proper assessment of the effect of climate change on water resources 
and flow characteristics, studies have been taken up by Central Water Commission, 
Brahmaputra Board and National Institute of Hyderology with active participation of reputed 
academic institutes. The study is being coordinated by Central Water Commission. The 
objective of the study is to examine the effect of climate change on water resources with a 
view to (a) assess the extent of likely changes in the water availability and the flow 
characteristics, (b) evaluate the effect of such changes on the performance of the water 
resources system, and (c) to identify appropriate measures to address the effect of climate 
change on water resources. 
With a view to mitigate the effect of possible changes in flow characteristics and ensure 
optimal utilization of available water resources, various measures for conservation of water, 
including creation of storages, traditional water conservation practices, rainwater harvesting 
and recharge to ground water are taken up by the respective State Governments. The 
interlinking of rivers project also aims at optimal utilisation of surplus flood water. The 
National Water Policy envisaged that efficiency of utilisation in all the diverse uses of water 
should be optimised, an awareness of water as a scare resource be fostered, the water resources 
be conserved and the availability augmented. 
Fresh guidelines for recruitment of loan recovery agents 
* 406.   SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN:
DR (SHRIMATI) NAJMA A. HEPTULLA: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
whether RBI has issued fresh guidelines to be followed by the private banks for recruitment 
of loan recovery agents; 
if so, the details in this regard and whether these guidelines are drafted in consultaries; with 
the private banks; 
how the antecedents of recovery agents are being verified by the Banks; 
what role the State police plays in this regard; and 
how the fresh guidelines are different from the old guidelines? 

Written Answers to [22 APRIL 2008] Starred Questions   21 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (ej On 30th 
November, 2007, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) placed draft Guidelines on engaging recovery 
Agents by scheduled commerical banks on its website, for feedback. Based on the feedback 
invited from individuals/organizations and banks, etc. including private sector banks, the 
guidelines have been revised and a second draft has been issued on 25th March, 2008 for 
feedback. Both the draft guidelines are available on RBI website www.rbi.org.in. Some of 
the important changes made in the second draft, inter-alia, include that: 
> Banks to ensure that the agents engaged by them in the recovery process carry out,
on a periodic basis, verification of antecedents of their employees—win,«. may
include police verification; 
The recovery agent would be required to carry an identity card issued by the bank or *.he 
recovery agency and also a copy of the notice/authorisation letter from the bank; 
Banks would be required to ensure that the notice/authorisation letter issued by then should 
also include the telephone numbers of the relevant recovery agents; 
Banks would also be required to record convention between the recovery agents and the 
customers; 
> Banks to place updated list of recovery agents on their websites;
> Where the bank is convinced, with appropriate proof, that the borrower is continuously
making frivolous/veatious complaints, it may continue with the recovery proceedings
through the Recovery Agents — even if a grievance/complaint is pending with them. 
In case where the subject matter of the borrower's dues might be sub-judice, banks 
should exercise utmost caution, as appropriate, in referring the matter to the recovery 
agents, depending on the circumstances of the case; 
> Banks should have an appropriate mechanism in place to utilise the services of the
credit counsellors for providing suitable counselling to the borrowers where it becomes
aware that the case of a particular borrower deserves sympathetic consideration. 
Post office savings scheme 
*407. SHRI D. RAJA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state:
whether it is a fact that recently the withdrawals from the various post office savings 
scheme are more than the deposits, leading to a negative growth; 
if so, the details thereof and reasons therefor; and 
what is Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. During 
April 2007 — February 2008 the withdrawals (including redemptions on maturity) under 
the Small Savings Schemes in Post Offices and Banks were Rs. 1,35,735 crore as against the 
gross small savings collections of Rs. 1,23,725 crore.  
The trend in collections, inter-alia, reflect investor's preference for other alternative savings 
instruments. Over a period of time, investment options available have increased both in 
number and variety, offering a wider choice to investors for their savings. De-regulation of 
the interest rates relating to banks, financial institutions and debt markets have also contributed 

22    Written Answers to [RAJYASABHA] Starred Questions 
to directing the flow of savings into instruments other than small savings schemes of the 
Government, which are subjected to administered interest rates.  
With a view to sustaining investor's interest in the small saving schemes, the features of 
the schemes are reviewed from time to time and various improvements and amendments in 
the schemes are introduced. Some of the recent measure includes; 
(i) The benefit of Section 80C of the Income Tax Act, 1961 has been extended to the
investments made under 5 — Year Post Office Time Deposit Account and Senior
Citizen Savings Scheme, with effect from 1.4.2007.  
(ii) Introduction of a bonus at the rate of 5 per cent on the deposits made under Post
Office Monthly Income Account (POMIA) scheme on or after 8th December,
2007 upon the maturity of the deposit. 
(iii) With effect from 1-8-2007, the maximum deposit ceiling of Rs. 3.00 lakh and Rs.
6.00 lakh under the Post Office Monthly Income Account (POMIA) scheme has
been raised to Rs. 4.5 lakh and Rs. 9.00 lakh in respect of single and joint accounts 
respectively. 
Financial restructuring of BHPV 
* 408.     SHRI TAPAN KUMAR SEN:
SHRI MOHAMMED AMIN:

Electronic medium of banking 
*409. SHRI TARIQ ANWAR: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state:
whether it is a fact that Government has decided to encourage use of electronic medium for 
banking; 
if so, the details of the facilities provided by the banks; 
whether all the facilities available in the urban areas are provided in the rural areas too; 
if not, the reasons therefor; and 
what are the steps Government is taking to provide those facilities in rural areas also? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) and (b) Reserve 
Bank of India has been encouraging the use of electronic banking. It has taken a number of 
steps in this drection, which include:—  
1. Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS):
RTGS is a fully secured electronic funds transfer system where banks and customers
can receive payments on real basis. Out of 71, 781 bank branches as on 31.03.2007,
around 44,000 bank branches now accept requests for remittance through RTGS
system for customer transactions as well as inter-bank transactions. The RTGS system
is tor transaction of value over Rs. 1 lac and other transactions take and alternate
channel of electronic funds transfer.
2. National Electronic Funds Transfer (NEFT):
This is a nation-wide retail electronic payment system to facilitate funds transfer
between the networked bank branches in the country. It is a deferred net settlement
system with six settlement cycles on week days and three settlements on Saturdays.
This facility is currently available at around 44,000 bank branches throughout the
country.
3. Electronic Clearing Services (ECS):
Two variants were developed—one named ECS (Credit Clearing) and the other called
ECS (Debit Clearing). While ECS (Credit Clearing) is used for making payment of
salary, pension, dividend and interest, ECS (Debit) is used for collection payments
by utility service providers like electricity, telephone bills as well by banks for
receiving principal/interest repayments for housing and personal loans from
borrowers. This facility is currently available at 68 centers.
4. Automatic Teller Machines (ATMs):
Through networking of ATMs the ATM/Debit Cardholders can obtain cash round
the clock. Networking of ATMs across the country enable the bank to provide
anywhere and anytime banking services to the customers.
(c) to (e) The normal facilities of electronic banking are extended at rural and urban
centres which are in the network and under Core Banking Solution (CBS). All banks have 
indicated their plans to complete full migration to CBS in phases in the next one to four 
years.

Agricultural land under Wealth Tax 
♦414. SHRI NARESH GUJRAL: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
whether it is a fact that agricultural land, which is being used for agricultural purposes but 
falls under the Municipal limits/jurisdiction, is subject to Wealth Tax; and 
is so, whether Government is thinking of exempting it from Wealth Tax? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) Urban land is an 
asset chargeable to wealth-tax under the Wealth-tax Act, 1957. "Urban land" under section 
2(ea) of the Wealth-tax Act means land situated—  
(i) in any area which is comprised within the jurisdiction of a municipality (by whatever
name called) or a cantonment board and which has a population of not less than ten thousand 
according to the last preceding census of which the relevant figures have been published 
before the valuation date; or 
(ii) in any area within such distance, not being more than eight kilometres from the local
limits of any municipality or cantonment board referred to above, as the Central Government 
may, having regard to the extent of, and scope for, urbanisation of that area and other relevant 
considerations, specify in this behalf by notification in the Official Gazette, 
but does not include—  
land on which construction of a building is not permissible under any law for the time being 
in force in the area in which such land is situtated; or 
the land occupied by any building which has been constructed with the approval of the 
appropriate authority; or 
any unused land held by the assessee for industrial purposes for a period of two years from 
the date of its acquisition by him; or 
any land held by the assessee as stock-in-trade for a period often years from the date of its 
acquisition by him.

airline like weather, airport congestion, ATC delays. The delays include consequential delays,

functioning at Mumbai on round-the-clock to coordinate various flight handling departments and

Formulation of guidelines for debt recovery 
2979. SHRI M.V. MYSURA REDDY: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
whether Government has formulated any debt recovery guidelines for Nationalised/ 
Private/Foreign Banks in the country; 
if so, the details thereof; 
whether it is a fact that horror activities are being adopted by the private banks with the 
borrowers for recovery of outstanding loans; and 
if so, the reasons therefor and the steps being taken or porposed to be taken by 
Government to prevent such type of humiliation with the people of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN 
KUMAR BANSAL): (a) to (d) Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has taken up with banks, for 
appropriate action, the media reports in respect of the banks engaging musclemen and 
harassing the defaulting customers for recovery of loans. In many such instances the excesses 
were alleged to have been committed by the recovery agents of the respective banks. The 
number of complaints of alleged harassment received against ICICI Bank has been more. 
In view of the alleged harassment of customers by ICICI Bank's recovery agents, and the 
judgement of Hon'ble Supreme Court, on an appeal (No. 267 of 2007) filed by ICICI Bank 
Ltd. against the order of the Allahabad High Court in respect of a case filed by one of the 
borrowers of the bank Smt. Prakash Kaur, the bank was advised by RBI in August, 2007 to 
investigate and take action against the recovery agents involved, review at the highest levels 
the system of appointing/reviewing performance of recovery agents, undertake comprehensive 
review of coustmer complaints, etc. In October 2007, RBI also advised the Bank that if such 
incidents recur in future, RBI would be constrained to take stem action. 

52    Oral Answers [22 APRIL, 2008] to Questions 
In the Mid-Term Review of Annual Policy Statement (dated October 30,2007), RBI has 
observed that in view of the rise in the number of litigations against banks for engaging 
recovery agents in the recent past, it is felt that the adverse publicity could result in serious 
reputational risk for the banking sector as a whole. RBI has urged banks to follow prescribed 
guidelines while engaging recovery agents and has clarified that complaints received regarding 
abusive practices followed by a bank's recovery agent would invite serious supervisory 
disapproval. RBI would consider imposing a temporary ban (or even a permanent ban in 
case of persistent abusive practices), for engaging recovery agents, on those banks where 
strictures have been passed/penalities have been imposed by a High Court/Supreme Court 
or against its Directors/Officers with regard to the abusive practices followed by their recovery 
agents. . 
RBI has also placed on its website, on 30th November, 2007, draft Guidelines for Banks 
engaging Recovery Agents for feed back. Based on the feedback received from banks/ 
individuals/organisations, the guidelines have been revised and a second draft has been 
issued on 25th March, 2008 for feedback. These guidelines cover various operational issues 
concerning engagement of recovery agents by the banks, methods to be followed by them 
for recovery of dues, training for the recovery agents, procedure for taking possession of 
property mortgaged/hypothecated to the banks, etc. The banks have also been advised to 
strictly abide by the codes pertaining to collection of dues.

3011. SHRI AMIR ALAM KHAN: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
whether Government proposes to reduce cess on petrol and diesel in all the States of the country;

whether any estimate has been made in regard to the likely impact of such uniform-sales tax on

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI S.S. 
PALANIMANICKAM): (a) Taxes on sale of petrol and diesel, including levy of additional duties 
on petrol and diesel in the form of cess, State Development Tax and additional Sales Tax by some 
States, is a State subject by virtue of Entry 54 of State List of the VII Schedule of the Constitution 
of India. As per the agreed decision of the Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers 
(EC) regarding petrol and diesel, these are taxed outside Value Added Tax (VAT), under the

†3019. SHRI LALIT KISHORE CHATURVEDI: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
whether it is a fact that value of dollar has been in continuous depreciation particularly 
compared with rupee in the entire global scenario;

of continuous increase in CRR and the purchase of dollar securities by the Reserve Bank 
of India; and

relations with G-8 countries? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN 
KUMAR BANSAL): (a) The average exchange rate of the Rupee against US Dollar, on a 
day-to-day and month-to-month basis, has shown two-way movements during 2007-08 and

(b) The exchange rate policy in recent years has been guided by the broad principles of
careful monitoring and management of exchange rates with flexibility, without a fixed target 
or a pre-announced target or a band, coupled with the ability to intervene, if and when 
necessary. RBI closely tracks the exchange rate movements and has responded appropriately 
by intervention in the domestic foreign exchange markets depending upon overall market 
conditions. 
The Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) was increased by the RBI, in phases, from 6 per cent to 
7.5 per cent during 2007-08, and is being increased in two phases by 25 basis points each 
w.e.f. April 26,2008 and May 10,2008 reaching it upto 8 per cent. Changes in CRR primarily
address liquidity concerns in the domestic economy and not the external value of the rupee.
(c) Exchange rate movement is an on-going process. India's trade with other countries,
including G-8 countries, depends upon various factors, such as exchange rate, relative price 
levels, levels of productivity and trade arrangements.

3022. SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: 
SHRI VIJAY J.DARDA: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
whether the Prime Minister's Economic Advisory Council has recommended for the 
creation of National Mission for Financial Inclusion to provide better access to institutional

KUMAR BANSAL): (a) and (b) The Committee on Financial Inclusion, set up under the 
chairmanship of Dr. C. Rangarajan, Chairman of the Prime Minister's Economic Advisory 
Council, has recommended Government of India to consider constituting a National Mission 
on Financial Inclusion (NaMFI) comprising representatives from all stakeholders. The 
purpose of the Mission is to achieve universal financial inclusion within a specified time

and Rural Development (NABARD).

and Rs. 5 crore respectively, in each Fund in March, 2008. RBI is expected to contribute its

Closure of Banks in Rural Areas  
3035.SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
SHRI HARISH RAWAT:  
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state:  
whether a large number of rural branches of scheduled commercial banks have been closed 
down in the country during the past few years; 
if so, the details thereof;

and 
if so, the reasons for closure of bank branches in rural areas? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (S HRI PAWAN 
KUMAR BANSAL): (a) to (d) As per data furnished by RBI, the number of 'Rural' branches 
of Scheduled Commercial Banks have reduced from 32,244 (as on 30.6.2003) to 30,628 (as 
on 30.6.2007). At the same time, the 'Semi-Urban' branches have increased from 14,904 to 
16,296, 'Urban' branches from 10,733 to 12,914 and 'Metropolitan' branches from 8,744 to 
11,913.  
The reduction in the number of rural branches is not necessarily on account of closure of 
rural branches. Based on population category, the b anks are classified in four group i.e. 
'Rural' (upto 9999 population), 'Semi-Urban' (from 10,000 to 99,999 population), 'Urban' 
(from 1 lakh to 9,99,999 population) and 'Metropoli tan' (10 lakh and above population). 
Earlier the bank branches were classified based on the 1991 Census and these have now 
been reclassified by the RBI on the basis of the 2001 Census (made effective 2006 onwards). 
Therefore, the branches, which were earlier classif ied as 'Rural' as per 1991 Census data, 
may have moved into a higher population category on account of increase in population of 
the respective centres resulting in the re-classification of the branch into 'Semi-Urban'.  
Besides, apart from re-classification due to increase in population of the particular centre, 
there are also instances where certain centres, which were earlier classified as 'Rural', were 
brought into the jurisdiction of the adjoining Municipality/Municipal Corporation and thus 
classified as "Urban/Metropolitan' depending on the population of the Municipality/Municipal 
Corporation.  

Written Answers to [22 APRIL 2008] Unstarred Questions   87 
Under the extant Branch Authorisation Policy of RBI, closure of even loss making branches 
in rural centres having a single commercial bank branch (excluding Regional Rural Bank 
branch) is not permitted, as the closure would render the centre unbanked. The proposals 
for closure of a rural branch at a centre served by more than one commercial bank branch are 
required to be submitted to RBI by banks in the Annual Branch Expansion Plan after obtaining 
approval of District Consultative Committee (DCC). RBI considers these proposals on a 
case-to-case basis and closure of rural branches is approved only under exceptional 
circumstances like adverse law and order problem, natural calamities etc. 
To ensure greater financial inclusion, especially in the rural areas and for increasing the 
outreach of the banking sector, RBI has permitted banks to provide banking services using 
the services of Business Facilitator/Business Correspondents. In rural centres, where it is 
felt that there is limited business potential for opening a bank branch, banks have started 
reaching out by providing banking services based on smart card technology.

3049. SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: W i l l  the Minister of PET ROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state:  
whether Government is aware that black-marketing of subsidized LPG cylinders is going on 
unabated in Delhi and rest of the country;

the godowns of oil companies only; 
if so, whether Government makes on the spot survey of these depots; 
whether Government is also aware that subsidized LPG is also finding place in hotels and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL 
GAS (SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL) (a) to (e): The possibility of blackmarketing of subsidized 
domestic LPG cylinders by some unscrupulous elements cannot be ruled out due to the wide gap 
between the retail price of LPG for domestic use and the market price for commercial LPG  
In order to stop blackmarketing/diversion of domestic LPG cylinders, the Government 
has enacted "Liquefied Petroleum Gas (Regulation of  Supply and Distribution) Order, 
2000"and formulated "Marketing Discipline Guideline s, 2001" which provides for penal 
action against LPG distributors indulging in diversion/blackmarketing of LPG.  
Whenever OMCs receive complaints, these are investi gated and if the complaint is 
established, suitable action is taken against the L PG distributor(s) in accordance with the 
provisions of the Marketing Discipline Guidelines ( MDG). MDG provides for following 
action against the distributor:—  
Fine of Rs. 20,000 plus the price of LPG diverted at commercial rates for 1st offence. 
Fine of Rs. 50,000 plus the price of LPG diverted at commercial rates for 2nd offence. 
Termination of the distributorship for 3rd offence. 
In addition to the action taken by the OMCs, State Govenments are empowered under the 
LPG (Regulation of Supply & Distribution) Order, 20 00 promulgated under the Essential 
Commodities Act, 1955 to taken action against blackmarketing/diversion of domestic LPG 
Similarly, the Weights and Measures Departments of the States/UTs initiate initiate legal 
action against those LPG distributors diverting LPG cylinders. The State Governments have 
been alerted from time to time to take steps against the blackmarketing/diversion of domestic 
cylinders for unauthorized usage.

Government have issued advertisements cautioning the public that use of domestic LPG 
for non-domestic purposes is illegal, dangerous and against national interest. Through these 
advertisements, cooperation of the general public h as also been sought to report any 
irregularity/malpractice to the OMCs.  
The officials of OMCs carry out random checks at distributors godowns, delivery points, 
as well as en-route to ensure that no misuse takes place. The distributors of OMCs are under 
strict instructions to check the weight of cylinders at their godowns before delivery, and only 
cylinders with the specified weight are to be deliv ered to the customers. The distributors 
have also been instructed to ensure that the seals are verified & shown to the customers at 
the time of delivery. In case any under-weight cyli nder is received by the customer, such 
cylinders are replaced free of charge by the OMCs.  
Public Sector Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) have r eported that at present, there is 
no overall shortage of LPG in the country and LPG supplies to distributors are being made 
by the OMCs through indigenous production and impor ts in accordance with the genuine 
demand of customers registered with the LPG distrib utors.  
However, OMCs had reported backlog in LPG supplies in certain States in the country, 
due to a combination of factors viz., reduction in supply of bulk LPG compared to the target 
by Reliance Industries Limited (RIL) & Essar Oil Limited in January-February, 2008, delay 
in movement of bulk LPG by rail from Jamnagar to the Northern Region, increased demand 
in the States due to severe cold which resulted in panic booking by the customers, strikes by 
contract labour, agitational activities, delays in berthing of vessels at Haldia Port due to 
reduced draft, bandhs etc.  
Government had advised OMCs to liquidate the backlog in the country by operating the 
bottling plants on holidays and during extended hours. Increased bottling is also done during 
the working days for early clearance of backlog.  
At present, OMCs have not reported any backlog in supply of LPG in the country. OMCs 
are monitoring the situation on a day-to-day basis and corrective action is being taken wherever 
required.

Subsidy on cooking gas  
3068. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: 
SHRI RAHUL BAJAJ:  
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state the reasons 
for not excluding the above poverty level households from subsidies on cooking gas?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL 
GAS (SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL): While abolishing the Administered Pricing Mechanism 
(APM) effective 1st April 2002, the Government had decided that pricing of all other 
petroleum products, except PDS Kerosene and Domesti c LPQ would be determined by 
market factors. In order to provide Kerosene and LPG at affordable prices, the Government 
formulated subsidy schemes which are in operation since April 2002.  
The prices of Domestic LPG and PDS Kerosene, which are considered as common man's 
fuels, have not been increased since November, 2004 and March, 2002 respectively.  
However, in view of the steep increase in internati onal oil prices since 2004, the 
Government has taken a conscious decision not to pa ss on the burden of the increase in 
international oil prices to the consumers. To deal with the steep escalation in international 
oil prices, the Government has adopted the principl e of'equitable burden sharing' between 
the Government, the oil PSUs and the consumers so as to protect the interests of the common 
man as also the financial health of the OMCs (Oil Marketing Companies). The Government 
has issued Oil Bonds and the Upstream Oil Companies have contributed by offering price 
discounts on crude oil and petroleum products, to partially compensate the under-recoveries 
of the OMCs.

3069. SHRI NAND KISHORE YADAV: 
SHRI AMAR SINGH:  
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state:  
whether Government has examined the provisions of t he gas supply contract signed by 
Reliance Industries Ltd. (RIL) with Reliance Natura l Resources Ltd. (RNRL) on 12 
January, 2006 pursuant to a Scheme of Arrangement approved by the Bombay High Court 
on 9 December, 2005; 
if so, the details thereof; 
whether RIL has agreed to supply Natural Gas to RNRL under production sharing contract 
(PSC) or any part of the natural gas of Government or other contractors; and 
the rationale in different stances taken by Governm ent while dealing with the two court 
cases viz NTPC-RIL and RNRL-RIL? 

112    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL 
GAS (SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL): (a) and (b) The Gas Supply Master Agreement (GSMA) 
dated 12th January, 2006 signed by Reliance Industries Limited (RIL) with Reliance Natural 
Resources Limited (RNRL) is purely a private arrangement entered into between the two 
parties pursuant to a Scheme of Arrangement approved by the Bombay High Court. However, 
the Government received a proposal dated 14th April, 2006 seeking approval of the gas 
price of US $ 2.34 per MMBTU at the defined "Delivery Point" under the said GSMA. The 
proposal stated that the execution of GSM A was subject to satisfaction of number of conditions 
precedent including approval by the Government to the price. The approval was sought for 
the price which was to be used for cost recovery, profit sharing and all other purposes under 
the Production Sharing Contract (PSC). 
The Government examined the proposal in the light of PSC provisions regarding valuation 
of gas, principles of arms length price, prevailing gas prices under other PSCs and did not 
agree to the proposal on the ground that price was not derived on competitive arms length 
principles and asked the contractor to send a revised proposal in accordance with PSC 
provisions. RIL submitted another application dated 18.5.2007 seeking approval to the price 
and the formula after having followed a bidding process, which was accepted by Empowered 
Group of Minister (EGOM) with slight modifications. 
RIL had agreed to supply natural gas to RNRL from Block K.G-D-6, through this GSMA. 
The PSC for this Block has been signed by RIL with Government of India (GOI) and 
another company Niko Resources Limited (NRL) which holds ten (10) per cent 
participating interest'(PI) in this Block. Under the PSC, the Contractor has freedom to market 
the gas produced from the Block, subject to various provisions of the PSCA as per PSC, 
contractor is entitled to sell its participating share of gas in cost petroleum and profit petroleum. 
The government is entitled to received share in profit gas available after recovery of the 
Contract costs, correspoding to pre-defined Investment Multiple. The RIL's entitlement of 
gas can be known only after quantification of the costs of extraction and development. Hence, 
in the case of RIL vs RNRL, in order to protect the interests of the government and the 
public at large, the Government has filed an intervention application before the Hon'ble 
Mumbai High Court for vacating the present restraint on RIL on committing gas from 
KG-D6 Block to any third party (other RNRL and NTPC). 
The Mumbai High Court had pronounced judgement on 15th October, 2007 in case of RIL vs 
RNRL and the two companies were given four months time to renegotiate, reconsider and 
settle afresh the terms of Gas Supply Agreement. Since there was no settlement, the 
Government considered it appropriate to intervene at expiry of this period in order to protect 
the interests of the Government and public at lar£,e, in terms of early.start of production from 
KG-D6 block, entitlement of Government share of gas and freedom to commit/sell gas to 
third parties other than RNRL and NTPC.

Nepal territory on these rivers such as, Saptkosi High Dam at Barahkshetra, Bagmati 
Multipurpose project at Noonthar, Kamala Dam at Chisapani, etc., to store the flood water. 
The Government of India has set up a Joint Project Officer (JPO) at Biratnagar (Nepal) in 
August 2004 to undertake field surveys and investigations in order to conduct feasibility and 
prepare the project reports of the aforesaid projects. 
State Government of Bihar has also undertaken the raising, strengthening and extension 
of existing flood embankments on the rivers, namely, Kosi, Gandak, Burhi Gandak, Lalbakeya, 
Baghmati and Kamla Balan to contain the flood waters, with Central assistance. 
As per the information available from the Government of Bihar, the State Government 
has identified six intra-state rivers links to divert the excess flood water from flood affected 
to rain-deficient areas in order to overcome the problem of floods in North Bihar and drought 
in South Bihar.

Upgradation of canal infrastructure in Punjab 
3097. SHRI DHARAM PAL SABHAPWAL: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES 
be pleased to state: 
whether it is a fact that century old canal irrigation network of 14,500 kms in the State of 
Punjab has outlived its life; 
whether it is also a fact that State Government has made specific requests to the Central 
Government for upgradation of canal infrastructure; 
if so, what are the details of recommendations made by the State Government; and 
the step being taken to give clearance to the State Government for upgradation of canal 
infrastructure in the State? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI 
JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (d) The Hon'ble Chief Minister of Punjab in a 
letter dated 27.02.2008 has sought financial assistance for anti water logging measures in 
Punjab including canal relining and has enclosed a concept note in this regard. The note 
mentions of century old canal network in the State. No extent of the network which has 
outlived its life has been mentioned. 
The concept note mentions that on the basis of recommendations made by a Central 
Ground Water Board Team which visited the water logged areas of Muktsar, Ferozpur and 
Faridkot districts during the month of September-October 2007, a comprehensive Anti-Water 
Logging Project has been prepared comprising of schemes concerning new surface drains, 
sub-surface drains, installation/rejuvenation of lift pumps, correction in deficiencies of existing 
drains by constructing new bridges or by deepening and widening of the existing drains, 
laser leveling and other miscellaneous issues such as pissiculture, bio-drainage and 
energisation of shallow tube wells. The estimated cost of the above project is about Rs. 300 
crores. The concept note further mentions that the results of the above measures would not 
last for a long time if no corrections are made at the source of seepage and has therefore 
proposed relining of Rajasthan Feeder from RD 179000-496000 and Sirhind Feeder from 
RD 124000-434587 as it would save a substantial amount of canal water for Rajasthan and 
Punjab and also check water logging in the adjoining areas of the canals to a large extent. 
The estimated cost for the relining works out to about Rs. 425 crore for Rajasthan Feeder 
Canal and Rs. 225 crore for Sirhind Feeder Canal as per the concept note. Thus the total 
anticipated cost of the proposal as mentioned in the note is Rs. 950 crores.

Contamination of ground water 
3100. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be 
pleased to state: 
whether the underground water of certain districts of Andhra Pradesh are being affected with 
the contaminants such as flouride, Arsenic, iron, salinity etc.; 
if so, the details of the districts affected by contaminants and the measures initiated at village 
level to tackle the situation during the last three years; 
whether the resultant affects that have helped the people to source potable water from 
underground; and 
if so, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI 
JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (d) The report/findings of Central Ground 
Water Board regarding ground water situation in Andhra Pradesh indicate that: 
(i) the quality of shallow ground water in the coastal tracts of Andhra Pradesh varies
widely from fresh to saline, while ground water in deeper acquifers is generally
saline. In East Godavari, West Godavari, Krishna, Nellore and Prakasham districts
also ground water in deeper acquifers has been found to be saline.
(ii) Salinity in ground water has been observed in shallow as well as deeper acquifers
in western part of Kurnool district and central part of Guntur district.
(iii) Flouride concentration beyond 1.5 mg/litre has been observed in parts of Nalgonda,
Prakasham, Anantpur, Kadapa, Mahaboobnagar, Krishna, Kurnool, Rangareddy,
Karimnagar and Guntur districts.
(iv) Iron concentration in excess of 1.0 mg/litre has been reported from Chittoor,
Kadapa, Rangareddy, Hyderabad, Karimnagar and Medak districts.
(v) No arsenic contamination has been reported so far in the State.
(vi) The data available with Central Ground Water Board is shared with State
Government to facilitate the process of remedial measures to be taken in view of
the situation arising out of contamination of ground water.

SHRI D. RAJA (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, the survivors of the 1984 Bhopal gas tragedy 
have been camping out at Jantar Mantar for the last 23 days. They have walked 800 km from Bhopal 
to Delhi and this is their second such padayatra in two years. Two years ago, the Bhopal gas tragedy 
survivors arrived on foot from Bhopal. Their demands were not for compensation. Their demands 
were for long-term rehabilitation — medical,  
t[Transliteration in Urdu Script].

social, economic, for environmental cleanup, and clean water. Like all other victims of a 
terrible crime, their demand was also that the law must be made to take its course in 
apprehending the guilty companies — Union Carbide and Dow. During their last visit to 
Delhi, the hon. Prime Minister had met them and assured that he would do everything within 
his power and within law to help them and to hold Union Carbide and Dow Chemical 
accountable. These promises have not been kept. In these two years of unkept promises, 
more than 720 people have died because of gas-related illnesses. Several children have been 
born with grotesque deformities — with cleft palates, missing fingers, mental retardation, 
and weak limbs. Sir, these are our children. And this is the second disaster — the tragedy 
that is unfolding only because this country continues to pretend as if the problems in Bhopal 
will disappear if we shut our eyes and ears. This is very sad. Today, Dow Chemical is trying 
to influence the highest offices in the country — bargaining for immunity in return for 
investments. The Government failed to do even the basic minimum to demonstrate that it is 
serious about tackling crimes regardless of the stature of the criminals. Dow has registered 
three pesticides by manipulating some of the Indian Agricultural Ministry officials. This was 
found in February, 2007. Till date, the guilty officials from Dow have not been caught or 
punished nor has the illegal registration been revoked. Dursban, Sir, one of the three pesticides, 
is provenly dangerous to children. It cannot be sold for home or garden use in the United 
States of America but it is freely available in India. Two years ago, the Minister of Industry 
and Commerce approved the purchase of UNIPOL, a Union Carbide technology, by Reliance 
from Dow.....

Inconvenience caused to public due to B.R.T. Corrid or in Delhi  
DR. CHANDAN MITRA (Nominated): Sir, I rise to draw the attention of the House to 
one of the most ill-conceived transit scheme ever to be launched in the city of Delhi. As a 
result of which the people of the entire Southern part of the city have been suffering for the 
last several months. Now, their tolerance level has gone beyond all acceptable limites. This 
scheme, known as the Bus Rapid Transit (BRT), is pl aying havoc with people and their 
lives. Eight people have already died, several scores have been injured, vehicles have been 
damaged, and all the protests have fallen on absolutely deaf ears. The very idea of making 
buses running in the middle of the road and reducin g the space available for cars to 3.3 
metres on either side is a completely ill-conceived idea. Now, you have buses running in the 
middle of the road and bus stops in the middle of the road. We were told that the idea is to 
help the bus passengers, commuters and pedestrians.  Pedestrians are unable to reach the 
middle of the road to catch those buses. That is ca using total confusion. The time taken to 
cross a 5.8 km. stretch has come to two hours. Around thousand trees have been cut down 
along this entire Corridor in order to make space for this absolutely scatter-brained scheme. 
And, more trees are going to be cut because this is only the first corridor. We are told that 
there will be six more corridors. This is a matter of great concern that public opinion is not 
taken into account. People are not consulted, stakeholders are not involved, only a few IIT 
Professors, with completely no idea of how traffic runs in the city, having seen some so-
called schemes very successful in Bogota, in Columbia, and at some places in Canada have 
imposed that scheme on the people of Delhi. This is  a matter of great shame. The whole 
consultation process was scrapped. The RWAs were not taken into account; parking space 
has not been created. Thus, a complete may them has  been caused. We were told that this 
scheme would bring down pollution. But when cars ar e leaving their engines idling with 
ACs inside, you can very well imagine how much more  pollution is being caused on the 
streets of Delhi because cars are stuck, as every n ewspaper and TV channel is reporting. 
Even the bus passengers are grievously affected by the difficulties because the signalling 
system is completely weird. Through this House, I want to raise the demand that this scheme

Need to resume the production of vaccines by three P.S.Us  
SHRIMATIBRINDAKARAT (West Bengal): Sir, this is in connection with the reported 
decision of the Ministry of Health to stop producti on of vaccines meant for universal 
immunisation programme (UIP) and the public health system in three public sector vaccine 
units i.e., Pasteur Institute of India, Connor; the Central Research Institutes, Kausauli--H.P, 
and BCG Vaccine Laboratory, Chennai. Shockingly the annual plan of the Ministry of Health, 
2007-08, does not mention this at all. On the contrary, it praises the work of these units. This, 
then, has been done behind the back of Parliament which is highly objectionable. It is to be 
noted that all six basic vaccines for the UIP for millions of infants and children are produced 
in these units at a very low cost and there have been no complaints on the quality, potency 
and safety of the vaccines produced and supplied by these PSUs. Moreover, they have trained 
manpower and have the R&D capability that should be  the core of any public health 
programme. The Ministry is planning to start a vaccine park in Tamil Nadu, entrusted to the 
Hindustan Latex-what it has got to do with vaccines -at an initial cost of Rs. 150 crores. 
When already vaccine producing units exist in the p ublic sector with the necessary exper-
tise, what is the logic behind such a decision? It is reported that till such time as the new 
units start functioning by, at least, 2-5 years, the requirement of the Universal Immunisation 
Programme will be met by buying supplies from priva te companies. This will have an ad-
verse impact on the model of self reliance. It is well known that many foreign pharma com-
panies are trying to enter the public health vaccin e programme. It will be in the national 
interest if the Government permits production in the PSUs and upgrades their technologies 
to provide the best required vaccines for our children.

Increasing Child Mortality Rate in KBK districts of Orissa  
SHRI RAMA CHANDRA KHUNTIA (Orissa): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, through you, I 
want to draw the attention of the House to the increasing number of deaths of children in 
the KBK districts of Orissa. The death rate of children is increasing in the tribal areas of 
Orissa in spite of the Integrated Childhood Management Programme being implemented 
in the sixteen districts. Around 30,023 ASHAKARMIs have been appointed. About Rs. 
6285.516 lakhs have been spent on it. Again, Rs. 32,67,6902/-have been spent on the 
Mother Protection Scheme, and Rs. 6 crores have been spent on the Norway-India Joint 
Programme. But, the death-rate of children in Koraput, Malkangiri, Nabarangpur, 
Mayurbhanj, Rayagada and Kandhamal is like this. In 2004-05,526 children died, whereas, 
the figure was 657 in 2005-06. In 2006-07, the figure was 674. In Koraput, 833 children 
died in 2004-05, and in 2005-06,1105 children died. In Malkangiri, 585 children died in 
2004-05,604 children died in 2005-06, and 792 children died in 2006-07. In Mayurbhang 
district, 1750 children died in 2005, 1751 children died in 2006, and 1934 died in 2007. 
In Nabarangpur, around 1473 children died in 2005, 1486 children died in 2006, and 
1627 children died in 2007. In Rayagada district also, 1537 children died in 2005, 1592 
children died in 2006, 1585 died in 2007. This clearly indicates that in tribal areas of 
Orissa, the child mortality rate has increased. The situation is very serious. In fact, it is a 
matter of great public concern. 
In addition to all these above stated schemes, the long-term action plan for KBK districts, 
for which the Central Government sanctioned a lot of money, has been implemented. Ad-
equate funds were also given by the Central Government for health care, education and 
childcare. The Orissa Government has completely failed to protect the children in tribal 
areas, especially in KBK districts. 
While expressing concern, I urge upon the Central Government to send a high-level Com-
mittee to inquire into this matter. The House may also give direction to the State Govern-
ment to take immediate and appropriate steps to protect the children in the tribal areas of 
Orissa.

Need to develop terminal facilities at Nagarcoil Station in 
Tamil Nadu  
SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I would like to bring to the notice of 
the Government about the long-pending proposal of developing terminal facilities at Nagarcoil 
station for trains from Kanniyakumari in Tamil Nadu. Kanniyakumari is one of the famous 
tourist places in Tamil Nadu, situated at the South ern tip of our country, evoking many 
foreign and domestic tourists all over the year. Even though Kanniyakumari is enriched with 
its traditional historic moments and many panoramic natural views like morning Sun seeming 
to arise from the sea, etc. it has no proper connec tivity with many cities and towns in the 
country. Due to insufficient platform and terminal facilities at Kanniyakumari and at Nagarcoil 
Railway station for the trains being operated from Kanniyakumari, and heavy congestion as 
a result of introduction of some new trains, the ma intenance of trains has become very 
difficult at Nagarcoil Station. In order to operate more trains from Kanniyakumari and main-
tenance of the same, a plan of action was made to improve the terminal facilities at Nagarcoil 
station. But, unfortunately, that planned proposal has been pending with the Government for 
a long time. In view of historic status of Kanniyakumari, which is the Southern end of our 
country, there is a need for providing more facilities for maintenance of new and the existing 
trains. Therefore, I request the Government to implement the proposal of developing termi-
nal facilities at Nagarcoil station, without any further delay.

Removal of Sukhoi 30 MKI fighter planes from Lohegaon Airbase, Pune, due to lack  
of spare parts  
SHRI SANJAY RAUT (Maharashtra): Sir, I would like t o draw the attention of this 
august House that, as reported, most of the SUKHOI 30 MKI fighters based at Pune Lohegaon 
airbase have been grounded by the Indian Air Force for want of spare tyres. The Indian Air 
Force has given the reason for this as 'technical upgradation.' There are two squadrons and 
only 10-12 Sukhois in the two squadrons are in a functional state and to make off the fighters 
functional. Sir, the Indian Air Force urgently requires adequate number of tyres to meet the  

Special  [22 APRIL 2008]  Mentions   151  
shortage so that it does not prevent the Indian Air Force from using the operational SUKHOIs 
to restart sorties over Western Maharashtra and nearby areas.  
Sir, the seriousness of the urgent requirement of spare tyres could be gauged by the fact 
that it has reportedly led to sending a four-member delegation of the Defence Ministry officials 
to Russia to seek spare parts, including tyres for the fighters.  
Sir, the situation now demands that the Defence Minister should inform the outcome of 
the above visit of the Defence Ministry officials and ensure that henceforth the shortage of 
spare parts and tyres for the fighters would be tak en care of by the Ministry well in 
advance.  
Need to stop telecasting of Astrological prediction s by 
Television Channels  
SHR1 SHANTARAM LAXMAN NA1K (Goa): Sir, on a number of television channels, 
programmes related to future predictions of individual prospects regarding financial, social, 
political, business, etc., are made in which people are misinformed and misguided, resulting 
in people remaining unduly complacent or unnecessarily worried. One can understand the 
concept of freedom of speech and expression but the freedom should not be stretched to take 
undue advantage of vast number of our illiterate masses and tender minds of our young men 
and women who are on the threshold of planning their academic or professional life.  
In the name of astrology, standard one-line predict ions are conveyed, which lines, are 
attributed to the people on one 'rashi' today and to the other the next day.  
People of certain 'rashis' are told not to wear clothes of a particular colour  and that 
certain days or numbers are auspicious to them without any rational basis. People are told to 
add certain alphabets in their names for better prospects.  
Predictions regarding film careers of actors, their matrimonial and extra-marital matters 
are made with spicy sentences.  
Predictions regarding illness are very dangerous and it causes immense harm to the society.  
When certain days are specified as bad for the people of certain 'rashis', such people may 
refuse to avail of opportunities which may be avail able to them on such days, or, students 
may not go for interviews for jobs if they are called on these days.  
In an era of scientific temper, which our Constitution enjoins upon us and which has also 
been reiterated in the Common Minimum Programme of the UPA, it is unfortunate that our 
country is being taken for a ride by such people and further our Government is also tolerating 
it.  I urge upon the Government to put a halt to such prgrammes.  
Need to release central assistance under Post-matric Scholarship for other 
Backward Classes students to the State of Maharashtra  
SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE (Maharashtra): Sir, the heading of my Special Mention is 
'Sanction and release of Central Assistance under Post-Matric Scholarships for other Backward 
Classes.'  
Sir, the Maharashtra Government has submitted a proposal on 3rd January, 2002 to the 
Union Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment on the above subject. This scheme is

for sanction of an amount of Rs. 17183.35 lakhs during 1997-98 to 2002-03 under the scheme. 
The castes of V.J.N.Ts, S.B.C. categories in the State, are categorized as OBC in the Central 
list. This expenditure of Rs. 17183.35 lakhs has to  be reimbursed from the Government of 
India. But out of this, the Government of India has  only released Rs. 439.14 lakhs on 30th 
March, 2002 and the balance of Rs. 16,744.21 lakhs is still pending with the Government of 
India. During the financial year 2003-04, an expenditure of Rs. 16,622.15 lakhs is pending for 
reimbursement from the Government of India. Then, i n 2004-05, expenditure of Rs. 
20000.40 lakhs, and in 2005-06, an expenditure of R s. 14549.80 was to be reimbursed by 
the Government of India, and, during 2006-07, Rs. 1 6000 lakhs, and, in the year 2007-08, 
Rs. 17,992.20 lakh was to be reimbursed. As on today, an amount of Rs. 101908.76 lakhs is 
required to be reimbursed from Government of India. Therefore, the Government of India is 
requested to release this amount as soon as Possible for the provision of all the scheme for 
the Backward Classes in our State.  
Miserable condition of women in the country  
SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI (Nominated): Sir, my Special M ention is about the 
dismal condition of Indian women.  
According to the latest report of the Christian Medical College of Vellore, the average of 
146 per one lakh suicides committed by Indian women is much more than the world average 
of 14 per one lakh suicides by women.  
Every hour, ten Indians commit suicide and a hundre d attempt to commit suicide. The 
rate of increase in population is only 2.1 per cent  while the rate of suicides committed is 
much higher at 6.2 per cent.  
Nearly five crore Indians are victims of depression, which is caused by a market-driven 
economy, western style of living, TV channel programmes, the culture of malls, cut-throat 
competition and the culture of materialistic consum ption. Forty-seven per cent pregnant 
women are anaemic. The mortality rate of 540 per on e lakh amongst the Indian women is 
much higher than the world average of 17. Females taking part in economic activity constitute 
only 42.5 per cent while those involved in household work is 70 per cent. Iliteracy rate of 40 
to 42 per cent amongst Indian women even after 60 y ears of Independence is worrisome. 
Women labourers earn 27.6 per cent less than their male counterparts while taking part in 
economic activities. Every 77th minute a dowry death takes place. Every 53th minute, a case 
of molestation, eveteasing or rape is recorded. Six ty-seven per cent of Indian women are 
victims of domestic violence. Every third minute, an FIR is lodged for some offence against 
women. We strive for 33 per cent reservation for women in the elected bodies of the country, 
but the dismal scenario of Indian women is a cause of great concern to all of us.  
Government must seriously view this sad plight of Indian women.

Need to provide better roads and more pds depots for tribals in Bhadrachalam 
constituency of Andhra Pradesh 
SHRIMATI RATNA BAI TADAPATLA (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Chairman, Sir, due to 
lack of good means of transport, tribals have to face immense difficulties while commuting 
over small distances in Bhadrachalam, Andhra Pradesh. 
It is because of bad roads or no roads at places that the tribals have to walk up to 20 
kilometres of hilly track to fetch their ration from the PDS depots. Their children find it 
difficult to attend schools and they find it difficult to transport their produce to the market to 
get remunerative prices. Not only that, it adds immensely to their woes in case of an emergency, 
such as sudden illness or delivery cases. Due to non-availability of doctors near their place 
of residence, they are forced to carry the patient to far off places for proper treatment. 
Hence, Sir, I would urge, through you, the hon. Minister of Tribal Affairs to ensure good 
roads for transport and more PDS depots for tribals to reduce their miseries.

SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE (West Bengal): Mr. Vice-Ch airman, Sir, 1 rise t 
support the Appropriation (Railways) Bill, 2008. While speaking on the Bill, I would liket 
take clues from some of the speeches made by the hon. Railway Minister during the last tw 
years. Sir, I have also seen the Reports of the Sta nding Committee on Railways. It is n 
doubt a fact that there are certain positive develo pments in recent years in Railways. Alsc 
we are glad that the direct railway service with Bangladesh has been opened up and we ar 
anxiously waiting for opening up of Agartala train service. You have said that it will tak 
effect very soon. I would like to point out here that for several years the Indian Railways ar 
scaling down some of the Budgeted physical targets over various Plan Heads such as ne\ 
railway lines, gauge conversion, doubling, signalli ng, electrification, etc., at the Revise' 
Estimates stage. For example, the physical target f or construction of new line during th 
year 2007-08 has been reduced to 155 kms at Revised Estimate stage, which is nearly 70 pe 
cent of the budgeted estimated. During 2007-08, the  Railways had targeted 700 kms. of 
doubling, which was reduced to 500 kms. and the act ual achievements till end of March 
2008 was expected to be 453 kms. In the process of capacity augmentation of signalling 
there has been a shortfall in achievement of targets, particularly in rehabilitation works during 
2007-08 and the spillovers are likely to be completed by March, 2009.  
In a major policy deviation, the Railways are explo ring the public-private partnershi| 
(PPP). But have the Railways assessed as to how much resources and technology the public 
private partnership will bring? Have the Railways f ormulated a cogent policy defining all 
terms and parameters of PPP clearly? Have the Railw ays explored the possibilities of 
augmenting the capacities of their own production units before entering into public-private 
partnership?  
During 2001-02 and 2005-06, the Railways had drasti cally cut down class 'C and 
class'D' posts. I quote from the replies given agai nst Starred Question No. 224, dated 
14.3.2008 In reply, Laluji informed this House that the number of class 'C employees as on 
31.3.2003 was 8,92,890 and on 31.3.2006 the number came down to 886454; that is, there 
were a net reduction-of 6436. Similarly, during the  corresponding period, the number of 
class 'D employees came down to 5,14,250 from 6,07, 493, registering a net reduction of 
93,243 employees. Further, during the period 2001-0 2 and 2005-06, the Railways have 
surrendered 1,12,664 posts.  
The Indian Railway Catering & Tourism Corporation, which was entrusted with catering 
services, has virtually turned to be the Indian Railway Tourism Services. The Railways have 
awarded licences to corporate business houses for s elling hot and cold beverages, packed 
and cooked food items at the stations. The corporate houses, on the other hand, handed over 
the stalls to franchisees, thus, making clear profit without making any investments. On the 
other hand, after a lapse of 23 years, the Railways  have adopted a policy to evacuate the 
commission vendors from the stations. Strangely, wh ile the commission vendors are 
demanding licences on easy terms to run their small units on the stations, the Railways are
